quiz: Think about what an OS does for many programs at once, and what simpler view of the hardware it gives each program.

Asynchronous means it can happen at any moment, caused by a device rather than by the instruction now running.
A fault is fixable. Once the missing page is loaded, think about which instruction still has not finished its work.
Each interrupt or exception has a vector number. Think about what the CPU needs to find next once it knows that number.
Each stage loads the next one. Start from what runs when power first reaches the CPU.
A monolithic kernel keeps drivers and file systems inside the kernel. Recall which listed systems are known microkernels.
Compare a plain jump inside your program with crossing into a more privileged mode and back, plus its side effects.
libc keeps output in a user-space buffer for terminals. Think about what event makes it flush the buffer.

A program in an endless loop never calls the OS. Think about how the kernel can still take the CPU back.

Explain the CPU mode bit, what is forbidden in user mode, and why this protects programs and the OS from each other.

Mention vector numbers, the descriptor table pointed to by a CPU register, saving state on the kernel stack, and jumping to the handler.
Go stage by stage: firmware and POST, bootloader, kernel and initramfs, then PID 1 starting services and the login prompt.

Compare where drivers and services run, the speed of in-kernel calls versus IPC, and fault isolation and trusted code size.
Explain the idea of a hybrid kernel and describe how Windows NT and macOS XNU mix microkernel ideas with in-kernel speed.
Name tools like strace, perf trace and eBPF, the patterns to look for, the fixes like batching or buffering, and measuring again.
